ety.text: First use appears c. 1920, originally vitamine (1912), from Latin vīta (“life”) (see vital) + amine (see amino acids). Vitamine coined by Polish biochemist Casimir Funk after the initial discovery of aberic acid (thiamine), when it was thought that all such nutrients would be amines. The term had become ubiquitous by the time it was discovered that vitamin C, among others, had no amine component. In 1920, British biochemist Jack Drummond proposed that the final -e be dropped to deemphasize the amine reference.

senses.d: Any of a specific group of organic compounds essential in small quantities for healthy human growth, metabolism, development, and body function. They are found in minute amounts in plant and animal foods or sometimes produced synthetically, and deficiencies of specific vitamins produce specific disorders.
preceding a word or its initial letter, to imply that the referent benefits health or wellness
ex: Vitamin N: The Essential Guide to a Nature-Rich Life
I just follow three three Cs: clean living, chewing thoroughly, and a daily dose of vitamin Church

grp.label: organic compound essential to human health

ety.text: From Middle English vital, from Old French vital, from Latin vītālis (“of life, life-giving”), from vīta (“life”), from vīvō (“to live”). Doublet of jiva and quick.

senses.d: Relating to or characteristic of life.
ex: vital energies; vital functions; vital actions

But open converse is there none,
⁠So much the vital spirits sink
⁠To see the vacant chair, and think,
‘How good! how kind! and he is gone.’

senses.d: Necessary to the continuation of life; being the seat of life; being that on which life depends.
ex: The brain is a vital organ.
And doen the heavens afford him vitall food?
The transition to farming was vital for the creation of civilisation.

senses.d: Relating to the recording of life events.
ex: Birth, marriage and death certificates are vital records.
It is vital that you don't forget to do your homework.
Vocabulary is a vital component of educational success in both first and second language contexts.
spirits that live throughout, vital in every part
I ought to go upright and vital, and speak the rude truth in all ways.

senses.d: Capable of living; in a state to live; viable.
ex: Pythagoras and Hippocrates […] affirming the birth of the seventh month to be vital.

grp.label: relating to, or characteristic of life
necessary to the continuation of life
